policies.question: How long do I have to cancel, and does it depend on what was bought?
policies.rule: It depends entirely on the product type. Perpetual software: full refund within 30 calendar days of purchase. Software subscriptions: prorated refund within 7 calendar days. License-based (per user) subscriptions: prorated refund within 7 calendar days. Microsoft Marketplace SaaS: full refund within 72 HOURS, excluding metered charges. Dynamics 365 Business Central: within 7 days of purchase OR renewal.
policies.consequence: Quoting one number to a customer gets it wrong for three of the five product types. The subscription's own cancellationAllowedUntilDate field is the authoritative deadline for that particular subscription; this table tells you what to expect before you have one.

policies.question: A subscription created by an upgrade was cancelled and we were refused. Why?
policies.rule: A subscription created as the result of a partial upgrade INHERITS the cancellation window of the parent it came from. It does not get a fresh 7 days from the day it was created, and the window does not reopen until that subscription renews into a new term.
policies.consequence: The upgrade looks like a new purchase, so everyone expects a new window. If the parent was bought two months ago, the new subscription is already outside it on day one.

policies.question: Can I reduce seats on a software subscription?
policies.rule: No. Partner Center does not allow licence reductions on software subscriptions at all. If the count is wrong it has to be changed inside the seven-day cancellation window, by cancelling and repurchasing.
policies.consequence: Seat-based habits do not transfer. On a licence-based subscription a reduction inside the window is normal; on a software subscription there is no reduction path at any point, so an over-purchase is locked in for the term once the window closes.

policies.question: The customer will not pay. Are we still liable to Microsoft?
policies.rule: Yes. The partner is responsible for paying any outstanding amount regardless of whether the customer cannot or will not pay, including because of bankruptcy, dissolution, or a commercial disagreement with the partner. Nothing about the customer's situation moves the liability off the partner.
policies.consequence: An annual-term subscription sold to a customer who later defaults is a full-term debt the partner carries. The documented mitigations are to sell such customers a MONTHLY term, which can be cancelled at the end of any month, or not to sell to them.

policies.question: Can a cancelled Marketplace free trial be started again?
policies.rule: No. A Microsoft Marketplace free trial can be cancelled at any point during the trial period, but once cancelled it cannot be reinitiated.
policies.consequence: Cancelling to tidy up a customer's list destroys an evaluation that cannot be recreated. Let it lapse instead if there is any chance the customer wants it.

policies.question: Does a promotion's licence limit count licences another partner already sold to the same customer?
policies.rule: Yes. Promotion licence limits are enforced across partners for the same customer. If a promotion caps at 1000 and one partner has already sold 900, a second partner selling 200 gets the NON-promotional price.
policies.consequence: The second partner has no visibility of the first partner's sale and quotes a promotional price they cannot get. Verify eligibility first: the API returns the minimum, maximum, and how many licences remain.

policies.question: Does a promotion's minimum purchase requirement count licences the customer already has?
policies.rule: Yes. Eligibility against a minimum takes already-provisioned licences into account, including licences from another partner or bought web direct. A customer with eight licences and a promotion requiring ten qualifies by buying two more.
policies.consequence: Read the wrong way round this looks like the customer must buy ten. Quoting ten when two would do loses the deal or oversells it.

policies.question: What happens if the term I buy does not match the promotion's term?
policies.rule: The transaction goes through at the NON-promotional price. Promotions define their discount per term, and a mismatch is not an error.
policies.consequence: Nothing fails, so nobody notices until the invoice. Check the promotion's term and billing cycle against what you are actually buying.

policies.question: If I change a subscription's term mid-term, do we lose the promotion?
policies.rule: Not necessarily. A term duration can be changed mid-term to the options Partner Center offers, and if a promotion exists for the resulting term and billing cycle it is applied automatically. Mid-term changes take effect immediately.
policies.consequence: Make sure no scheduled changes are pending on the subscription before adjusting the term, or the two collide.

policies.question: A promotion id and a catalog item id look different. Which one is the limit counted against?
policies.rule: The promotion's product SKU, not the availability. A promotion id has a product:SKU:availability shape, and limits such as licence count are evaluated against the product:SKU part only.
policies.consequence: Different product SKUs carry different promotion ids, so a customer can hit the maximum on Microsoft 365 E3 and still get promotional pricing on E5. Assuming one shared pool understates what is available.
